description: We are Phoenix Protocol, a group of passionate A-Level students from Lahore Grammar School, Johar Town (LGS JT), Pakistan. United by our interests in science, technology, and innovation, we aim to tackle real-world challenges through research, creativity, and collaborative problem-solving. Through PyroScale, we hope to demonstrate how young innovators can harness NASA's Earth observation data and emerging technologies to develop meaningful solutions with global impact.
summary: PyroScale is an advanced geospatial analytics platform developed to ingest, harmonize, and model multi-decadal active fire hotspot data spanning from 2001 to 2026. The system processes historical satellite observations from NASA FIRMS feeds, applies geographic masking to filter high-latitude anomalies, and utilizes spatial reverse geocoding to link grid cells with precise territorial locations. To address the challenge of reliable environmental prediction, the platform implements rigorous rolling-origin backtesting frameworks and uncorrupted skill-scoring evaluations against seasonal baselines without data leakage. This is critically important because it delivers a robust, standardized temporal-spatial foundation for tracking and anticipating wildfire dynamics, empowering researchers and emergency managers to drive data-informed climate mitigation and disaster response strategies.
details:
For over two decades, NASA's satellite instruments have monitored active fires and thermal anomalies across Earth. However, a fundamental challenge complicates the analysis of long-term burning activity: MODIS and VIIRS observe the same phenomena with different spatial resolutions, detection sensitivities, and observing characteristics.

MODIS detects active fires at approximately 1 km resolution, whereas VIIRS offers 375 m fire-detection pixels, enabling it to identify smaller or less intense hotspots. Consequently, a change in recorded hotspot counts may reflect differences between instruments rather than an actual change in burning activity. Simply combining their observations risks producing misleading long-term trends.

PyroScale addresses this challenge through an integrated platform that processes, compares, and experimentally harmonizes NASA satellite observations into a continuous analytical framework spanning January 2001 to October 2026. Our objective is to make historical burning-activity patterns more comparable, transparent, and accessible.

What PyroScale Does:

PyroScale-AI transforms complex satellite observations into an interactive environmental analysis platform. Its primary capabilities include:

  • Historical Harmonization: Uses machine learning to estimate VIIRS-like historical hotspot counts from earlier MODIS observations.
  • Global Burning Activity Calendar: Organizes 310 months of satellite observations across 3,616 nonempty geographic grid cells, enabling seasonal comparisons, historical analysis, and anomaly detection.
  • Interactive 3D Globe: Allows users to explore worldwide hotspot activity, select geographic regions, search for locations, and visualize historical trends.
  • Forecasting: Provides evaluated 1–24-month NOAA-20 VIIRS hotspot-activity outlooks, with empirical uncertainty intervals where supported.
  • Environmental and Scenario Analysis: Integrates weather context and user-controlled hypothetical scenarios involving temperature, precipitation, human burning, and fuel management.
  • Data Accessibility: Offers downloadable datasets, geographic summaries, model-evaluation reports, and transparent documentation.

Our methodology follows a five-stage workflow.

Data Acquisition: We obtain NASA FIRMS thermal-anomaly observations from Terra MODIS, Suomi-NPP VIIRS, and NOAA-20 VIIRS through a publicly accessible archive mirror.

Preprocessing: Python and DuckDB pipelines perform confidence filtering, duplicate control, temporal aggregation, and data-quality checks. Observations are organized into monthly 3° × 3° geographic cells, preserving instrument identity and explicitly identifying missing records.

Machine-Learning Harmonization: We developed a Poisson LightGBM gradient-boosting model trained on 158 matched science-processed MODIS–VIIRS months. The model uses historical detection counts, geographic coordinates, and seasonal variables to estimate VIIRS-like observations rather than relying solely on a constant conversion factor.

Validation: Chronological training, development, calibration, and testing periods are combined with geographically held-out blocks. On later observations within the fitted geographic footprint, our model achieved a 15.8% reduction in mean absolute error compared with a fitted scaling baseline.

Visualization: Processed observations and model outputs are integrated into a browser-based Three.js environment, enabling interactive geographic exploration, statistical comparisons, forecasting, and data exports.

PyroScale's central innovation is the integration of instrument-aware satellite processing, forecasting based on historical data and machine learning, nonlinear historical calibration, scientific validation, and interactive visualization into one reproducible analytical platform.

While NASA FIRMS provides authoritative satellite observations, PyroScale focuses on addressing the discontinuities that arise when comparing different generations of instruments.

Our approach incorporates geographically and temporally informed machine-learning calibration, explicitly preserves the distinction between observed and reconstructed data, and communicates model uncertainty and limitations.

Unlike a conventional hotspot visualization, PyroScale connects historical reconstruction with seasonal analysis, geographic exploration, forecasting benchmarks, and hypothetical environmental scenarios.

Its novelty lies in transforming fragmented satellite measurements into an accessible, evidence-based workflow rather than claiming to invent a new satellite instrument or machine-learning algorithm.

PyroScale aims to make long-term satellite fire observations more useful to environmental researchers, educators, students, and the wider public.

By improving the comparability of historical measurements where model performance supports it, the platform enables investigation of regional burning patterns, seasonal variability, and unusual periods of thermal activity.

Its interactive design reduces the technical barriers associated with working directly with large Earth-observation archives, while transparent uncertainty reporting encourages responsible interpretation.

Our long-term goals include incorporating additional satellite instruments, improving geographic resolution, integrating cloud-cover and observation-geometry information, expanding environmental predictors, and strengthening cross-regional model validation.

Ultimately, PyroScale seeks to complement existing satellite monitoring systems with an accessible platform for understanding historical global fire activity.

Programming Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3.

Machine Learning: LightGBM with Poisson objectives, NumPy, chronological validation, rolling-origin backtesting, seasonal benchmarks, and empirical uncertainty estimation.

Data Processing: DuckDB, Parquet, CSV, JSON, and Python-based aggregation pipelines.

Geospatial Technologies: Three.js, WebGL, Shapely, Natural Earth geographic boundaries, spatial intersections, and interactive SVG visualizations.

Data Sources: NASA FIRMS (Terra MODIS, Suomi-NPP VIIRS, and NOAA-20 VIIRS), the Source Cooperative FIRMS archive mirror, Natural Earth geographic datasets, and Open-Meteo environmental data.

Development and Testing: Git, GitHub. (Repository Linked in Demo)
